articles.title: Imaging of developmental, inflammatory, and benign or malignant neoplastic petrous apex lesions in children: what the radiologist needs to know.
articles.abstract: The petrous portion of the temporal bone is a complex pyramidal-shaped structure of the central skull base, which contains osseous, air cell, vascular, and neural structures in close proximity, making imaging interpretation challenging. A broad spectrum of lesions may involve this region, including inflammatory, neoplastic (benign or malignant), vascular, and osseous lesions. In the pediatric population, ongoing skull base maturation and normal anatomical variability further complicate imaging assessment and may mimic pathology. Cross-sectional imaging plays a central role, with CT providing detailed assessment of osseous structures and MRI offering superior soft tissue characterization. Familiarity with the normal developmental anatomy, common anatomical variants, imaging pitfalls, and characteristic imaging features of pediatric bone lesions is essential for accurate diagnosis and appropriate patient management. This review provides a structured overview of pediatric petrous apex lesions, emphasizing imaging protocols, normal developmental variants, and key imaging features across inflammatory, neoplastic, vascular, and miscellaneous entities.

articles.title: ESR Essentials: trauma whole-body CT imaging-practice recommendations by the European Society of Emergency Radiology.
articles.abstract: Major trauma is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, particularly among children and young adults, and rapid identification of life- or limb-threatening injuries through imaging is crucial. Whole-body CT (WBCT) is central in modern major trauma pathways, enabling early detection of critical findings to guide multidisciplinary decision-making. Our study suggests three evidence-based recommendations for WBCT in major trauma care. First, WBCT protocol selection should be tailored to haemodynamic status and injury mechanism rather than applied as a single universal protocol; incorporating split-bolus, dual-phase and triple-phase techniques, each offering different diagnostic strengths and trade-offs. Special considerations can apply in pregnancy, paediatric patients, and those with contrast allergy, who may require modified imaging strategies. Second, radiologists should play an active role in trauma multidisciplinary team (MDT) care, assisting in protocol adaptation and directly directing the trauma team to life-threatening injuries. Third, systematic, checklist-driven radiological reporting with defined communication pathways improves trauma diagnostics, increases reporting reproducibility and strengthens trauma decision-making. These recommendations are best implemented through locally agreed, mechanism and physiology-based WBCT protocols, supported by trauma-trained radiologists embedded in scanning processes and multidisciplinary trauma care. KEY POINTS: Whole-body CT enables rapid and comprehensive assessment of patients with major trauma and suspected multisystem injury. Radiologists play an active role in trauma team care through real-time CT assessment and early identification of life-threatening injuries. Modern trauma imaging should incorporate standardised, protocol-driven acquisition and structured image interpretation.

articles.title: Shear-wave elastography in rotator cuff tears: a systematic review of measurement properties, tissue-stiffness findings, and clinical interpretability.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Shear-wave elastography (SWE) may quantify rotator cuff mechanical properties, but its measurement performance and clinical interpretability remain incompletely established. This work sought to synthesize evidence on the feasibility, measurement properties, and interpretability of rotator cuff SWE in adults with rotator cuff tears (RCTs). MATERIALS AND METHODS: PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched. Eligible studies were in vivo primary studies in adults (≥ 18 years) with suspected or symptomatic rotator cuff disease in whom partial- or full-thickness RCT was confirmed by an imaging or surgical reference standard, including conventional ultrasound, MRI, CT, or arthroscopy, and/or studies including clinically relevant comparator shoulders or asymptomatic controls. Studies had to use ultrasound SWE with quantitative outputs, including shear-wave speed/velocity or modulus, in the supraspinatus tendon and/or rotator cuff muscles. RESULTS: Thirteen SWE studies were retained from 6273 records. Two primarily assessed reliability/repeatability. Intra-rater reproducibility was high in the primary reliability studies, including ICCs > 0.87 and 0.96, whereas inter-rater reproducibility was lower and variable, ranging from ICCs > 0.73 to 0.45. Eleven studies contributed construct-validity or known-groups evidence, one provided strict criterion-validity evidence against intraoperative passive stiffness, and two provided longitudinal postoperative evidence. SWE findings varied across tissue targets, devices, regions of interest, arm positions, comparators, and reference standards. Only one study explicitly defined chronicity, and direct postoperative/prognostic evidence was limited. CONCLUSIONS: SWE appears useful as a complementary quantitative imaging tool for selected rotator cuff tissue-characterization and measurement-property applications. However, inter-rater reproducibility, measurement error, chronicity assessment, and prognostic validity remain insufficiently established. KEY POINTS: Question Can shear-wave elastography (SWE) address the unmet need for reliable quantitative rotator cuff tissue assessment beyond conventional imaging in adults with tears? Findings Thirteen studies showed high intra-rater reproducibility but variable inter-rater reproducibility. Evidence for chronicity assessment and prognosis remained sparse and heterogeneous. Clinical relevance SWE may complement ultrasound or MRI by quantifying selected rotator cuff mechanical properties, but current evidence does not justify using it alone to determine tear chronicity, reparability, or prognosis.

Event-to-Payment Latency in Physicians With Imaging-Related Allegations: NPDB Reports Processed 2004-2025.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To characterize event-to-payment/report-processing latency among physicians with imaging-related allegations. METHODS: This retrospective cross-sectional study included National Practitioner Data Bank physician payment reports processed in 2004-2025, excluding state-fund reports. Imaging-related allegations were identified in either specific-allegation field. Latency equaled original report-processing year minus alleged-event end year, using onset year when end year was unavailable. Adjusted models included report characteristics and jurisdiction, with practitioner-clustered standard errors. Complementary analyses examined events in 2004-2010 and jurisdiction random effects. RESULTS: Among 199,060 eligible reports, 1,980 involved imaging-related allegations (1,852 physicians). Median latency was 4 years (IQR, 3-6); 47.0% had latency ≥5 years. The proportions were 43.7% (2004-2009), 42.9% (2010-2015), 46.1% (2016-2020), and 55.7% (2021-2025). Adjusted differences were +0.66 years for permanent injury and +0.48 for death versus nonpermanent injury; +0.38 for outpatient and +0.49 for mixed settings versus inpatient care; and +1.56 for judgment versus settlement/other. All corresponding 95% confidence intervals excluded zero. Age was associated with -0.16 years per decade-category increment. Among 562 reports for events in 2004-2010, median latency was 4 years and 44.1% had latency ≥5 years. The adjusted payment ratio per additional latency year was 1.021 (95% CI, 0.997-1.044; P=0.082). DISCUSSION: Paid reports involving physicians with imaging-related allegations frequently reflected care delivered years earlier. The payment association was small, imprecise, and not statistically significant. These selected paid-report data do not estimate litigation duration, future payment risk, or radiologist-specific performance.

articles.title: Predictive and risk stratification performance of CCTA-derived pericoronary adipose tissue radiomics for major adverse cardiovascular events: retrospective development and prospective validation.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the predictive efficacy and risk stratification potential of coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA)-derived pericoronary adipose tissue (PCAT) radiomics for major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs). MATERIALS AND METHODS: We retrospectively enrolled patients with suspected coronary artery disease (CAD) who underwent CCTA at our hospital between June 2017 and June 2020, with 5-year follow-up for MACE occurrence. Patients were grouped by MACE status. Machine learning was applied to construct and compare three models: PCAT radiomics model, fat attenuation index (FAI) model, and clinical model. Prospective validation was conducted in 578 patients with suspected CAD undergoing CCTA, who were stratified into high- and low-risk groups by the optimal cutoff of the PCAT radiomics model. The predictive and risk stratification performance of all models was assessed. RESULTS: Fourteen PCAT radiomics features (5 first-order and 9 texture features) were finally screened. The PCAT radiomics model showed significantly superior MACE predictive performance over the FAI and clinical models (P < 0.001). Only the PCAT radiomics model identified significantly higher MACE risk in the high-risk versus low-risk group (HR=2.611, 95% CI: 1.806-3.775, P < 0.001), with progressively reduced MACE-free survival in the high-risk group during follow-up (P < 0.001). No such significant between-group differences were found in the FAI and clinical models (all P > 0.05). CONCLUSION: The PCAT radiomics model showed favorable performance for predicting the composite MACE endpoint, which was predominantly driven by worsening stable or unstable angina, and provided better risk stratification than the FAI and clinical models.

articles.title: Diagnostic accuracy of MRI-derived imaging biomarkers and machine learning-based classification in distal and myofibrillar myopathies.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To characterise and validate disease-specific muscle imaging patterns in distal and myofibrillar myopathies, quantify their diagnostic performance, and develop an imaging-based classification framework incorporating machine learning. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Muscle MRI and CT scans from a multicentre national cohort of patients with genetically defined distal and myofibrillar myopathies were retrospectively analysed. The pattern of muscle involvement for each disease entity was described, and its sensitivity and specificity calculated. Supervised machine learning algorithms were trained using muscle scores and imaging-derived features, and their diagnostic performance was compared using balanced accuracy. RESULTS: A total of 165 patients (mean age 48 ± 16 years; 87 men), including 138 molecularly confirmed cases spanning 19 disease genes, were analysed. Overall, 6350 muscles were systematically evaluated. Key findings included early biceps femoris short head involvement in GNE myopathy, "fat pockets" in myotilinopathy, and early flexor hallucis longus involvement in desminopathy. All imaging patterns showed high sensitivity and specificity (from 75 to 100%). Among the tested machine learning models, XGBoost achieved the highest performance, correctly distinguishing among 11 genetic disease entities with a balanced accuracy of 69%. CONCLUSION: Distal and myofibrillar myopathies demonstrate reproducible disease-specific imaging signatures with high diagnostic accuracy. Integration of these imaging biomarkers into a machine learning framework enables systematic prioritisation of likely genetic diagnoses and may facilitate diagnostic work-up in these heterogeneous inherited muscle disorders. KEY POINTS: Question How accurately do muscle MRI patterns distinguish distal and myofibrillar myopathies, and how do imaging features perform in an updated MRI-based diagnostic algorithm? Findings Disease-specific muscle MRI patterns showed high diagnostic accuracy, while XGBoost achieved the highest balanced accuracy among machine learning models for imaging-based disease classification. Clinical relevance Refined muscle MRI patterns provide diagnostically useful imaging biomarkers in distal and myofibrillar myopathies. Their integration into machine learning-based classification models may facilitate precision diagnostics and guide targeted genetic testing.

articles.title: MRI for the detection of hip abductor tendon tears in symptomatic patients with total hip arthroplasty following a lateral surgical approach.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of MRI for detecting clinically suspected hip abductor tendon tears in symptomatic patients after total hip arthroplasty and to evaluate the association between specific MRI features and surgically confirmed tears. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective study included 36 patients with total hip arthroplasty who underwent revision surgery for a suspected abductor tendon tear and had preoperative MRI available. Intraoperative findings served as the reference standard for the presence of partial or full-thickness tears of the gluteus medius (Gmed) and gluteus minimus (Gmin) tendons. Two readers evaluated MRI for tendon integrity (intact, partial-thickness, or full-thickness tear). Associations between tendon defects, peritrochanteric fluid, tendon signal abnormalities, and Gmed/Gmin Goutallier grades with surgical findings were analyzed using regression models to calculate odds ratios (ORs). RESULTS: For detection of abductor tendon tears, Reader 1 achieved sensitivities of 0.86-1.00, specificities of 0.93-1.00, and accuracies of 0.92-0.97, while Reader 2 achieved sensitivities of 0.86-1.00, specificities of 0.90-1.00, and accuracies of 0.89-1.00. Imaging findings associated with partial- or full-thickness tears included tendon defects (Gmed: OR = 35.5, p = 0.007; Gmin: OR = 30.0, p < 0.001), peritrochanteric fluid (Gmed: OR = 64.2, p = 0.01; Gmin: OR = 74.9, p = 0.01), and higher Goutallier grade (Gmed: OR = 2.34, p = 0.03; Gmin: OR = 4.75, p = 0.02). CONCLUSION: MRI demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy for detecting surgically confirmed hip abductor tendon tears in this selected symptomatic surgical cohort following total hip arthroplasty. Tendon defects and peritrochanteric fluid were significantly associated with partial- or full-thickness tendon tears. KEY POINTS: Question There is limited data on the diagnostic accuracy of MRI for hip abductor tendon tear detection following total hip arthroplasty. Findings MRI demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy for detecting surgically confirmed abductor tendon tears in symptomatic patients with total hip arthroplasty. Clinical relevance In symptomatic patients with clinical suspicion of an abductor tendon tear undergoing evaluation for revision surgery, MRI can be used to noninvasively assess the integrity of the abductor tendons after total hip arthroplasty.

articles.title: Generating patient-friendly radiology reports with a local large language model: expert evaluation of quality and readability.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To assess the feasibility of using a locally hosted large language model (LLM) to generate patient-friendly radiology reports while avoiding cloud transfer of report text. MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this retrospective study, 360 chest, knee, lumbar spine, and shoulder X-rays, and shoulder and abdominal ultrasound reports from Dutch primary care were included. Main report sections (n = 359) and conclusion sections (n = 350) were translated into patient-friendly versions using Gemma-3 (12B parameters) and assessed for accuracy and completeness on 5-point Likert scales. Readability was evaluated using text length and Flesch-Douma reading ease (FDRE) scores. Hallucinations were systematically documented. Statistical analyses included Kruskal-Wallis, Wilcoxon signed-rank, and paired t-tests. RESULTS: Patient-friendly conclusions achieved higher median accuracy scores than main reports (5 [Q1-Q3 5-5] vs 4 [3-5]), while completeness scores were high for both sections (5 [5-5]). Compared with original reports, patient-friendly reports were longer (median increase 65 words [48-84], p < 0.001) and had higher FDRE scores (mean increase 54.2 ± 18.8, p < 0.001). Overall, 71.0% of main reports and 96.0% of conclusions met predefined quality criteria (accuracy and completeness ≥ 4), while 48.0% of combined main report and conclusion sections met both quality and readability criteria (FDRE score > 60). Clinically relevant hallucinations occurred in 45 reports (12.5%). CONCLUSION: A locally hosted LLM demonstrated feasibility for generating patient-friendly translations of Dutch X-ray and ultrasound reports while avoiding cloud transfer of data, with better performance for conclusion sections than main reports. However, clinically relevant hallucinations remain a safety concern and indicate the need for clinician oversight and further evaluation before clinical implementation. KEY POINTS: Question Can a locally hosted LLM generate patient-friendly radiology reports while preserving data privacy and maintaining acceptable accuracy, completeness, and readability? Findings A locally hosted LLM generated patient-friendly report conclusions with higher quality scores than main reports, while clinically relevant hallucinations remained an important safety concern. Clinical relevance A locally hosted LLM has potential to generate patient-friendly radiology report translations without external cloud data transfer. Report conclusions appear to be the most promising initial application, although clinician oversight and further patient-centered validation remain essential before clinical implementation.

articles.title: The role of artificial intelligence in predicting late-onset intrauterine growth restriction in singleton pregnancies: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Late-onset intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) is difficult to detect and is associated with adverse perinatal outcomes. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the performance of artificial intelligence (AI) models, including machine learning (ML) and deep learning, for predicting late-onset IUGR in singleton pregnancies. METHODS: PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched for studies published during the past decade that used AI to predict IUGR. Nineteen studies including 13,379 pregnancies were analyzed. Sensitivity, specificity, likelihood ratios, and diagnostic odds ratios were pooled using DerSimonian-Laird random-effects models; the area under the summary receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was estimated in STATA. RESULTS: In the primary analysis (one model per study, k=17), pooled sensitivity was 0.83 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.74 to 0.89), specificity was 0.89 (95% CI, 0.85 to 0.91), the positive and negative likelihood ratios were 6.6 (95% CI, 5.3 to 8.1) and 0.22 (95% CI, 0.16 to 0.30), and the AUC was 0.93 (95% CI, 0.91 to 0.95). Estimates were unchanged when all model entries were included (k=51). No threshold effect or funnel-plot asymmetry was detected. Subgroup estimates for support vector machines, random forests, and logistic regression were similar but reflected indirect comparisons. CONCLUSION: AI/ML models showed high pooled discriminative accuracy for late-onset IUGR. However, the evidence derives mainly from retrospective, single-center case-control studies without external validation; calibration was reported in six of 19 studies and decision-curve analysis in none. These estimates are an optimistic upper bound, not evidence of superiority over current ultrasound practice.

articles.title: A new bone lesion or an aging marrow phenotype? Rethinking bilateral distal femoral sclerosis.
CT-Based Pulmonary Segment Delineation: An Imaging Informatics Review of Methods, Benchmarks, Robustness, and Clinical Deployment.
articles.abstract: Accurate bronchopulmonary segment delineation on computed tomography (CT) is essential for segmentectomy planning, computer-assisted thoracic interventions, and fine-grained quantitative lung analysis. However, segment-level parenchymal partitioning remains technically challenging because intersegmental boundaries are often subtle or indistinct on routine CT, requiring bronchovascular priors-particularly airway and vascular trees-to guide anatomically plausible delineation. This review presents an imaging informatics-based synthesis of CT-based pulmonary segment delineation, covering conventional multi-stage pipelines and recent deep learning frameworks, including convolutional neural networks (CNNs), graph neural networks (GNNs), implicit neural representations, and continuous spatial modeling parameterized by Gaussian mixture models (GMMs). We organize evaluation practices into three complementary categories: direct ground-truth-based metrics, indirect anatomy-referenced criteria, and reference-free plausibility or quality-control measures. We further review publicly available datasets, annotation protocols, and benchmark limitations that currently hinder reproducible and fair segment-level comparison. From a deployment perspective, we discuss clinical workflow requirements, robustness challenges, and the need for anatomy-aware and data-efficient methods. Illustrative analyses of a single cystic fibrosis (CF) case using a distance-based method show how removal of a segmental airway branch or omission of lobar constraints can substantially alter the resulting segment territories. These case-specific observations motivate broader robustness evaluation, uncertainty-aware quality control, boundary-level plausibility checks, and deployment-oriented validation beyond conventional overlap-based metrics.

articles.title: New heuristic method for cancer classification using gene expression data.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The aim of this research is to develop and evaluate a novel feature selection method based on a local search algorithm (LSFS) in combination with a genetic algorithm (GA) for cancer classification using high-dimensional gene expression data. METHODS: The study spanned a period between 2022 and 2024, using data from two medical research centers (Sofia, Bulgaria, and Moscow, Russia). More than 30,000 patient records were analyzed using six open datasets as source data. These datasets included information on blood, breast, colon, and other types of cancer from the GEO and TCGA databases. To prepare the data for analysis, the study employed techniques such as normalization, outlier elimination, and logarithmic transformation. Modern machine learning algorithms, such as random forests, support vector machines, and neural networks, were utilized to assess the effectiveness of the proposed method. RESULTS: The LSFS + GA method demonstrated the ability to maximize accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity, as well as other classification metrics. Specifically, classification accuracy improved by 8-15% depending on the dataset, sensitivity by 10-20%, and specificity by 5-10%. Additionally, there was a 12-18% reduction in noise in the data. The effectiveness of the model was demonstrated by a reduction in entropy, indicating an increase in classification confidence of 6-9%. Statistical analysis, including cross-validation and ANOVA, confirmed the statistical significance of the improvements achieved with the new method (p < 0.05). CONCLUSIONS: The developed algorithm enables a substantial reduction in computational complexity while maintaining, or even improving, classification accuracy. This is important for analyzing cancer data, as it helps to ensure more reliable results. The study's findings demonstrate the potential of combining local search methods with genetic algorithms to address high-dimensional classification problems in bioinformatics.

articles.title: A compliant granular jamming gripper for improved robot-assisted surgical instrument handling.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Granular jamming grippers (GJGs) offer high geometric adaptability and intrinsic safety for robot-assisted surgical instrument handling but struggle with thin, planar instruments. This study investigates whether external pinching through a passive and partly compliant force-leveraging linkage can enhance grasping performance while maintaining a compact and simple design. METHODS: The SCIP-GRIP, a novel GJG with an integrated Scott-Russell linkage to convert vertical down force into horizontal pinching, was developed. The performances of three gripper versions with varying pinching heights were compared to that of a non-pinching GJG across three instrument types: scalpel (flat), forceps (vertical surfaces), and scissors (undercuts). Both, holding forces and pickup success rates were evaluated using a Universal Testing Machine. Holding forces were measured 12 times per case, while success rates were assessed over 50 trials each. RESULTS: Pinching improves performance across all instruments, with the largest gains observed for scissors, achieving holding forces above 10 N. For forceps and scalpels, only the lowest pinching height yields significant improvements. Success rates for scissors and forceps remain at 100 %, while scalpel success improves from 4 % to 18 % only at low pinching height. Higher pinching heights fail consistently. Performance strongly depends on pinching height, with increased height reducing effectiveness. CONCLUSION: The SCIP-GRIP demonstrates that a passive Scott-Russell linkage can enhance GJG performance while preserving simplicity and safety but pinching below 3 mm is necessary. The design achieves comparable performance to active systems at lower complexity, though further improvements are needed to reliably grasp flat geometries.

articles.title: Temporal MRI appearance of postoperative healing after proximal hamstring musculotendinous complex repair.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To describe the temporal MRI features of healing during the first 4 months following surgical repair of complete tears of the proximal hamstring musculotendinous complex. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Consecutive case series. Professional football players with MRI-confirmed complete tears surgically repaired between May 2017 and December 2025 were retrospectively identified. Postoperative MRI examinations were obtained during routine clinical follow-up using 3-T systems. Two musculoskeletal radiologists independently evaluated longitudinal and transverse intratendinous clefts, scar maturation, edema-like signal, postoperative subcutaneous soft-tissue signal change, tendinous angulation, blunt muscle outline, and denervation-like signal. RESULTS: Twenty-four complete tears in 20 players underwent surgical repair. Fifteen tendons with an uncomplicated postoperative course comprised the primary descriptive cohort, yielding 43 MRI examinations. Longitudinal intratendinous clefts were observed in 11/15 (73.3%) of tendons, transverse intratendinous clefts in 13/15 (86.7%), postoperative subcutaneous soft-tissue signal change and tendinous angulation in 15/15 (100%), blunt muscle outline in 13/15 (86.7%), and denervation-like signal in 10/15 (66.7%). In the within-tendon analysis, longitudinal and transverse intratendinous clefts resolved by the last available MRI in 6/10 (60%) and 7/12 (58.3%) tendons, respectively. All 10 tendons with an initially immature scar progressed to a mature scar. Among six tendons with postoperative exacerbation, four showed extensive, prominent intratendinous clefts with marked PD-FS hyperintensity on the preceding MRI, associated with immature scar, intratendinous cavity, or persistent interstitial edema-like signal. CONCLUSION: Serial MRI demonstrated different temporal patterns of postoperative healing. Residual intratendinous clefts may coexist with a mature scar during tendon remodeling and do not necessarily indicate delayed healing.

articles.title: Work Stress, Burnout and Depression among Radiology Residents: The Moderating Effect of Environment.
articles.abstract: RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to explore the modulating role of work environment in the association of work stress with burnout and depression during standardized residency training (SRT) in China. STUDY DESIGN: Nationwide cross-sectional survey. METHOD: A nationwide cross-sectional online survey was conducted among radiology residents in China from December 2020 to April 2021. Participants self-assessed work stress, burnout, depressive symptoms, and work environment satisfaction. Multiple linear regression was used to examine whether the work environment modulated the associations between work stress and burnout and depression. RESULTS: Among 3666 radiology residents surveyed, the average age was 28 years, with 58% identifying as female. Approximately 25.8% reported experiencing burnout, while 24.4% indicated symptoms of depression. Work environment significantly modulated the association between work stress and burnout symptoms (β = -0.23, p = 0.004), but did not significantly moderate the association between work stress and depressive symptoms (β = -0.03, p = 0.423). CONCLUSION: This study found that the work environment significantly moderated the positive association between work stress and burnout among radiology residents, but not the association between work stress and depressive symptoms. A work environment characterized by a stronger sense of safety and a better workplace atmosphere may improve residents' satisfaction with the work environment, thereby enhancing work efficiency and well-being.

articles.title: Management of Chronic Subdural Hematoma in Thrombocytopenia: Middle Meningeal Artery Embolization - Based Strategies Versus Medical Management or Surgery Alone.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Thrombocytopenia complicates management of chronic subdural hematoma (cSDH), but no study has compared middle meningeal artery embolization (MMAE) with surgery or medical management in this population. We evaluated MMAE-containing strategies versus medical management or surgery alone in cSDH with platelets below 100×103/µL. METHODS: Using the TriNetX Research Network, we identified adults with cSDH and platelets below 100×103/µL (or below 50×103/µL for the severe-thrombocytopenia analysis). We performed three propensity-score-matched comparisons: standalone MMAE versus medical management and surgery plus MMAE versus surgery alone at platelets <100×103/µL; and standalone MMAE versus medical management at platelets <50×103/µL. The primary outcome was 90-day all-cause mortality; the secondary outcome was surgical evacuation (a composite of surgical evacuation or mortality at platelets <50×103/µL). RESULTS: After matching, cohorts ranged from 147 to 373 patients per group (standardized mean differences below 0.10 for nearly all covariates). At platelets <100×103/µL, standalone MMAE was associated with lower mortality than medical management (26.9% vs 37.3% hazard ratio 0.65 [95% CI 0.50-0.85]), and surgery plus MMAE was associated with lower mortality than surgery alone (20.5% vs 30.7%; hazard ratio 0.61 [95% CI 0.38-0.97]). At platelets <50×103/µL, the mortality comparison between standalone MMAE and medical management did not reach significance (34.2% vs 44.0%; hazard ratio 0.72 [95% CI 0.49-1.05]). Subsequent surgical evacuation did not differ significantly in any comparison. CONCLUSIONS: For patients with cSDH and thrombocytopenia, management strategies incorporating MMAE were associated with lower 90-day mortality than medical management or surgery alone. Prospective confirmation is needed, including in severe thrombocytopenia, where the mortality comparison did not reach significance.

articles.title: Endovascular Thrombectomy for Large Vessel Occlusion Stroke in Patients with Metastatic Cancer.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) for large vessel occlusion (LVO) stroke is supported by high-quality evidence, but the safety and efficacy of EVT for patients with concomitant metastatic cancer is unclear. We aimed to compare outcomes of EVT versus best medical management (BMM) for LVO stroke patients with metastatic cancer. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective cohort study of the 2016-2022 Nationwide Readmissions Database includes adult patients with LVO stroke (internal carotid, middle cerebral, or basilar artery occlusion) and metastatic cancer. Propensity score matching (PSM) was performed using 1-to-1 nearest-neighbor matching. The primary outcome was early functional independence at hospital discharge. Secondary outcomes included discharge to home, hospital length of stay, in-hospital mortality, and 180-day mortality. Outcomes were compared between those treated with EVT or BMM, and treatment effects are reported as risk differences (RD), risk ratios (RR), or hazard ratios (HR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). RESULTS: Of 5629 patients, 3590 remained after PSM (1833 EVT, 1757 BMM). Compared to BMM, EVT was associated with significantly higher rates of early functional independence (17.8% vs 8.7%; RD 9.1% [95%CI 5.1 to 13.1], RR 2.04 [95%CI 1.51-2.76]) and discharge to home (42.3% vs 34.1%; RD 8.2% [95%CI 3.2 to 13.2], RR 1.24 [95%CI 1.09-1.42]), with no difference in hospital length of stay (median 7 vs 6 days; P=0.34), in-hospital mortality (22.8% vs 24.3%; RD -1.5% [95%CI -5.6 to 2.6]), or 180-day mortality (30.3% vs 30.0%; HR 0.99 [95%CI 0.83-1.18]). Among patients who suffered in-hospital mortality (n=845), there was no significant difference in length of stay (median 5 vs 4 days, p=0.52). Among patients who survived the index hospitalization but later died within 180 days (N=185), EVT was associated with higher rates of interim functional independence (26.8% vs 12.7%; RR 2.11 [95%CI 1.02-4.37]). CONCLUSIONS: Among LVO stroke patients with metastatic cancer, EVT was associated with significantly higher rates of functional independence compared to BMM, without altering overall survival.

articles.title: Robust joint estimation of regional brain activity and inter-regional source covariance via full-structure covariance learning.
articles.abstract: Uncovering the mechanisms underlying cognition and brain disorders requires accurate regional source imaging and reliable characterization of inter-regional statistical dependencies. Traditional methods typically follow a two-stage pipeline that first performs source imaging and then calculates inter-regional dependence measures separately. Such a decoupled framework can propagate source-reconstruction errors to covariance-based network analyses, leading to biased source localization and distorted dependency patterns. To address these limitations, we propose a joint estimation method for regional brain source activity and source covariance via full-structure covariance learning, termed Joint Activity-Covariance Estimation via Full-Structure Covariance Learning (JAC-FS). JAC-FS constructs a Gaussian probabilistic model at the brain-region level and employs a full-structure source covariance matrix to represent regional source variance and inter-regional dependencies. In this covariance representation, diagonal entries encode marginal regional source variance, whereas off-diagonal entries quantify symmetric zero-lag covariance-based dependencies. These estimates are statistical associations and do not by themselves establish direct, directional, or causal physiological communication. A median-weighted covariance statistic suppresses high-energy artifacts, and convex surrogate optimization provides closed-form updates for source activity and source covariance. In addition, constrained noise estimation with diagonal floor protection, low-rank correlation constraints, and phased damped updates limits signal absorption and spurious covariance structure. Simulations showed that JAC-FS outperformed conventional algorithms in regional source localization, temporal recovery, source-covariance recovery against the simulated ground truth, and recovery of predefined short- and long-range covariance edges. In real MEG analyses, JAC-FS produced focal evoked source distributions and representative time courses together with evoked source-covariance patterns. These results establish JAC-FS as a unified framework for regional source imaging and zero-lag source covariance estimation.

articles.title: Applying Submental Ultrasound as a Screening Tool for Nasogastric Tube Removal Indication: A Pilot Study with Real-world Application.
articles.abstract: ABSTRACT: PURPOSE: Nasogastric tube (NGT) usage is common among inpatients. However, there is a lack of a convenient and objective tool for assessing a patient's swallowing function for NGT removal. The feasibility of using submental ultrasound for making decisions regarding NGT removal remains unclear. ABSTRACT: MATERIALS AND METHODS: This pilot study included patients with NGTs who underwent submental ultrasound examination for NGT removal from March 2023 to December 2025. Patients were divided into derivation and validation cohorts by different examiners. We first measured the resting mandible-hyoid distance and shortest distance when swallowing and then calculated the maximum hyoid bone displacement. ABSTRACT: RESULTS: In the derivation cohort, the maximum displacement was shorter in the NGT group (n = 31) than in the control group (n = 27) (1.26 vs. 1.83 cm, p ≤ 0.001), and the displacement was shorter in the "NGT not removed" subgroup (NG-NR, n = 21) than in the "NGT removed" subgroup (NG-R, n = 10) (1.09 vs. 1.63 cm, p = 0.006). In the validation cohort, the displacement was shorter in the NG-NR subgroup (n = 18) than in the NG-R subgroup (n = 6) (1.36 vs. 1.89 cm, p ≤ 0.001). In the derivation cohort, the displacement showed an AUROC of 0.805 for distinguishing between the NG-NR and NG-R subgroups. A cut-off value of 1.32 cm yielded a sensitivity of 80.0% and a specificity of 81.0%. In the validation cohort, the AUROC was 0.836. In the age- and sex-matched validation cohort, the AUROC was 0.831. The interrater consistency was good. ABSTRACT: CONCLUSION: Given its good discriminatory performance with regard to NG-R patient identification, interrater consistency, and convenience, submental ultrasound might be an effective screening tool for identifying suitable postacute NGT patients to start swallowing training before NGT removal.

articles.title: CT-based multimodal fusion model for preoperative clear cell renal cell carcinoma grading: A multicenter study.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To develop and evaluate a multimodal fusion framework for the preoperative World Health Organization/International Society of Urological Pathology (WHO/ISUP) low- and high-grade classification of clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), integrating clinical characteristics, deep learning (DL), and radiomic signatures extracted from corticomedullary phase (CMP) contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) images. MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this retrospective multicenter study, we evaluated a cohort of 1,052 patients with histologically verified ccRCC across four institutions. The data of the primary cohort (Center A, n = 665) were randomly divided into a training dataset (n = 465) and an internal validation dataset (n = 200). The data of 387 additional patients from three institutions (Centers B-D) constituted the independent external test set. Initial single-modality classifiers were developed via ensemble machine learning, utilizing clinical variables, multiscale radiomic data (capturing intratumoral, habitat, and peritumoral regions), and DL representations (2D, 2.5D, and 3D). A soft voting mechanism was subsequently applied to integrate the top-performing base models. Model interpretability was determined using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values, and overall diagnostic efficacy was quantified through receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. RESULTS: The weighted soft voting model (SoftVote-Opt) showed the numerically highest AUC among the evaluated fusion strategies and single-modality models. This model yielded AUCs of 0.761 (95 % CI: 0.675-0.839) and 0.745 (95 % CI: 0.675-0.813), with corresponding MCCs of 0.347 (95 % CI: 0.217-0.475) and 0.302(95 % CI: 0.205 -0.387), within the internal validation and external test sets, respectively. SHAP analysis revealed peritumoral 5 mm radiomic features as the primary determinants of the model's output, followed by intratumoral radiomic features, whereas deep learning and clinical features offered lower relative contributions. CONCLUSION: The multimodal fusion framework demonstrated moderate discriminatory performance across the internal validation and external test cohorts. These findings could be regarded as an exploratory study rather than evidence of established clinical superiority. The framework may provide complementary information for preoperative ccRCC grading. CRITICAL RELEVANCE STATEMENT: This study evaluates an exploratory multimodal fusion framework for preoperative ccRCC grading by combining clinical data, deep learning, and multiscale radiomic features. The framework may provide complementary non-invasive information for risk stratification.

articles.title: An uncertainty-aware deep learning-based registration model for adaptive lung cancer radiotherapy.
articles.abstract: To develop a deep learning (DL) based probabilistic 3D deformable image registration framework for uncertainty-aware dose accumulation in magnetic resonance imaging-guided radiotherapy (MRgRT) of lung cancer.Approach: We propose TransMorph-prob (TM-prob), a variational Bayesian model that predicts the voxel-wise mean and variance of dense displacement fields (DDFs). Two TM-prob models were trained on an internal CT dataset (725 patients) and a low-field MR-linac dataset (102 patients), and benchmarked against Monte Carlo dropout TransMorph (TM-MCD) and DIRUncertainty with B-spline initialization (ASDIR) on the DIRLAB 4DCT dataset (10 patients, 3000 landmarks), and an annotated MR-linac dataset (16 patients, 107 image pairs, 227 landmarks) with target and seven organ-at-risk (OAR) contours. Both datasets contained an additional 1239/13,289 algorithm-generated landmarks. Performance was evaluated using target registration error (TRE), Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), landmark- and voxel-wise expected calibration errors (LECE/ECE), and dose distributions derived from 2000 DDF samples per patient.Main results: On the DIRLAB dataset, TM-prob achieved a median TRE of \qty{1.8}{\mm}/\qty{2.8}{\mm} on manual/algorithm-generated landmarks, versus \qty{1.3}{\mm}/\qty{2.4}{\mm} for ASDIR and \qty{2.1}{\mm}/\qty{3.0}{\mm} for TM-MCD. On the MRI dataset, TM-prob achieved the median TRE of \qty{3.9}{\mm}/\qty{2.6}{\mm} and a mean DSC of 0.87, matching ASDIR (\qty{3.3}{\mm}/\qty{2.7}{\mm}, and DSC of 0.87) while outperforming TM-MCD (\qty{4.4}{\mm}/\qty{2.9}{\mm}, and 0.84). In uncertainty calibration, TM-prob achieved a LECE of \qty{1.74}{\mm}/\qty{0.30}{\mm} on MRI manual/algorithm-generated landmarks versus \qty{2.41}{\mm}/\qty{0.56}{\mm} for ASDIR and \qty{6.65}{\mm}/\qty{3.92}{\mm} for TM-MCD, and an average contour ECE of 5.8% versus 7.0% and 21.2%. Two patients with indistinct GTV boundaries exhibited substantially wider target D95 distributions, demonstrating that calibrated DDF uncertainty translates into clinically relevant dose-coverage uncertainty.Significance: TM-prob is an end-to-end DL model, achieving fast, well-calibrated, uncertainty-aware registration for lung cancer patients, enabling reliable DDF uncertainty propagation into dose accumulation for clinical decision-making in online adaptive radiotherapy.

articles.title: Generative structure-guided denoising diffusion probabilistic model for MR to CT image synthesis in radiotherapy planning.
articles.abstract: Radiotherapy (RT) planning uses magnetic resonance (MR) imaging for soft tissue information, while computerized tomography (CT) imaging is necessary for dose calculation. Synthetic CTs generated from MR images streamline the clinical workflow by reducing the need for an actual CT acquisition while minimizing radiation exposure, enabling adaptive RT workflows. Appraoch: We propose a radiotherapy planning model combining stable structure-guided denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) with MRI conditioning, for generating synthetic CT (sCT). The model combines a hybrid network with a dynamic guidance mechanism, conditioned on MR, to direct the reverse diffusion process and preserve structural details. The model integrates both a denoising and a refinement network, while the guidance strength adapts at each timestep based on the noise level. The training process includes a weighted structure-guided loss function that combines the DDPM noise loss with a dynamic guidance regularizer term for sCT image generation, with a refinement network. Main results: Evaluated on three paired MR/CT datasets (head and neck, brain), our model outperforms recent MR to CT synthesis models, showing the best performance in image quality based on the Mean Absoluate Error (MAE) in Hounsfield units, as well as improved Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) and Gradient Magnitude Similarity Deviation (GMSD) compared to other DDPM and GAN approaches. When comparing tumor segmentation quality, it achieves the best results in Dice score (0.76 ± 0.04) for segmented tumor regions in the generated sCT images. Finally, it achieves the best Mean Square Error (MSE) of 10.1 ± 2.6 Gray in the head and neck cohort, when evaluating dose planning on sCT, with a Conformity Index (CI) of 0.61 ± 0.02 and a Homogeneity Index (HI) of 0.10 ± 0.02. Significance: Performance shows promise in integration for radiotherapy in head and neck, as well as in brain cancers.

articles.title: Anatomical correlates of delivered TIS fields across deep and cortical targets.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: The objective of this study was to quantify inter-individual variability in target-region TIS envelope amplitude and to examine its associations with anatomical features across deep and cortical targets. APPROACH: We built individualized finite element head models for 502 healthy HCP participants aged 22-35 years and evaluated five target ROI-montage pairs: hippocampus (two montages), left and right thalamus, and motor cortex. For each target ROI-montage pair, we quantified mean TIS envelope amplitude within target region (EA mean , V/m) and the target-to-brain envelope-amplitude ratio (TBR) as measures of target-field magnitude and spatial selectivity, respectively. Two prespecified global volume ratios were assessed with Pearson correlations, and 20 anatomical features were evaluated using two-stage LASSO-OLS models with an 80:20 internal hold-out split. Bootstrap selection frequencies were calculated for the EA mean models. MAIN RESULTS: EA mean showed substantial inter-individual variability (CV = 28.1-40.0%). Brain-TIV ratio and GM-head ratio were positively correlated with EA mean across all five target ROI-montage pairs (r = 0.281-0.420; all p < 0.001), with directions compatible with CSF-related current shunting. Pairwise EA mean correlations across the five target ROI-montage pairs were high (r = 0.749-0.957). Five two-stage LASSO-OLS models yielded in-sample R 2 values of 0.185-0.282. For TBR, MC1 showed the strongest model fit (R 2 = 0.311; hold-out R 2 = 0.267), while no predictor reached p < 0.05 in either thalamic model. Global predictors appeared repeatedly in the deep-target models. In MC1, the significant set also included skull-head ratio and W-scalp thickness (MC1), neither of which was significant in the deep-target models. The two hippocampal montages (H1 and H2) differed by 31% in EA mean , and their predictor sets reaching OLS p < 0.05 showed modest overlap (Jaccard = 0.33). SIGNIFICANCE: This population-scale computational dosimetry analysis quantifies how fixed TIS currents and montages translate into target-field magnitudes across individual head models. The results distinguish the anatomical correlates of delivered amplitude from those of spatial selectivity and provide quantitative information for anatomy-informed TIS planning.

articles.title: Angle-domain null subtraction imaging from beamformed plane-wave data.
articles.abstract: Null subtraction imaging (NSI) narrows the apparent lateral response bycombining fields produced with a zero-mean apodization and two DC-offset variants.Usually, NSI requires channel data and flexible beamformers (Receive-NSI). We investigateAngle-NSI, which operates on per-angle images during coherent plane-wave compounding.Approach. A matrix formulation was used to distinguish receive-domain and angle-domainnull subtraction expressions and to identify their independent computational components.A small-angle model gives a physical interpretation of the angular null. The method wasevaluated using a simulated point target, experimental resolution phantom targets, anopen microbubble (MB) traces dataset and two in vivo carotid acquisitions. Anglesampling, noise, phase jitter and target position were swept in simulation. A synchronizedGPU benchmark compared the complete reconstructions. Six beamforming methods werecompared: delay-and-sum (DAS), coherence-factor-weighted DAS (CF-DAS), minimumvariance beamforming (MV), delay-multiply-and-sum (DMAS), Receive-NSI andAngle-NSI.Main results. Angle-NSI reduced the simulated -6 dB lateral width from 0.226 mm forDAS to 0.116 mm, compared with 0.009 mm for Receive-NSI, while the axial width was0.720 mm for these three methods. The lateral narrowing was confirmed on anexperimental resolution phantom. Angle-NSI had shorter reconstruction time thanReceive-NSI and the lowest post-delay processing time among the nonlinear methods. Inpower Doppler, microbubble trace widths were reduced by 50.2% for Receive-NSI and30.9% for Angle-NSI compared to DAS. On a phantom and in vivo, both NSI variantsreduced generalized contrast-to-noise ratio relative to the conventional methods.Significance. Angle-NSI provides simple post-processing of per-angle beamformed images.It narrows the apparent lateral response at low computational cost, at the expense ofB-mode detectability: this makes it a well-suited alternative for high-resolution powerDoppler applications.

articles.title: Three-dimensional computational evaluation of water-to-air mass stopping power ratio for therapeutic helium-, carbon-, oxygen-, and neon-ion beams and its application to patient-specific quality assurance.
articles.abstract: Current dosimetry protocols recommend a constant water-to-air mass stopping power ratio, sw,air, of 1.126 with an uncertainty of ±1.5% for light ions, irrespective of ion species and energy. This study aims to develop a computational framework to calculate three-dimensional sw,air distributions of helium-, carbon-, oxygen-, and neon-ion beams for patient specific quality assurance (PSQA), and to systematically investigate spatial variations in sw,air under clinically relevant conditions. Approach. A computational framework was developed to calculate three-dimensional sw,air distributions based on the Bragg-Gray approximation, together with three-dimensional dose distributions for treatment planning. The framework was validated against published datasets for a mono-energetic carbon-ion beam. Treatment plans were generated using helium-, carbon-, oxygen-, and neon-ion beams for rectangular targets with varying spread-out Bragg peak (SOBP) widths and depths, as well as for bone and soft tissue, head and neck, and ocular cases. The corresponding sw,air distributions were calculated in a water phantom and compared with the recommended value of 1.126. Main Results. The mean sw,air within the target increased for shallower targets with narrower SOBP widths. For all ion species, sw,air increased toward the distal end of the SOBP, with larger variations observed for heavier ion species. In neon-ion irradiations for shallow targets, sw,air occasionally exceeded the ±1.5% uncertainty range in a limited region near the distal end of the SOBP. In all other cases, sw,air remained within the uncertainty range. Similar trends were observed in clinical cases. Based on these results, when considering the mean sw,air within the target, the suitable fixed values were 1.128 for carbon and oxygen ions and 1.129 for helium and neon ions. Significance. The proposed computational framework enables three-dimensional, plan-specific evaluation of sw,air and provides a practical approach for improving the dosimetric accuracy in charged-particle therapy with helium, carbon, oxygen, and neon ions, especially for PSQA.&#xD.

articles.title: Artificial intelligence-enabled detection of vascular perfusion defects on ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) scintigraphy for pulmonary embolism.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Accurate interpretation of planar ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scintigraphy, used for diagnosing pulmonary embolism (PE) based on PIOPED/EANM guidelines, requires objective assessment of mismatched V/Q defects. Manual delineation of V/Q defects is time-consuming, subject to interobserver variability, and rarely performed in practice, limiting standardized reporting and quantification of disease burden. To address these challenges, we evaluated four modern AI models for automated segmentation of vascular perfusion defects in planar V/Q scans and compared their performance to human annotators. APPROACH: We retrospectively identified 2,118 patients who underwent planar V/Q scans at The Ottawa Hospital (June 2019-February 2023). Six standard projections (ANT, POST, LAO, RAO, LPO, RPO) were included. Four 2D neural networks (U-Net, nnU-Net, Swin UNETR, and a Bottleneck Transformer U-Net [BTU-Net]) were trained on 1,313 patients (7,878 projections) and validated on 329 (1,974 projections) using physician-annotated defects. A hold-out test set of 46 high probability patients was used to evaluate segmentation quality, and defect detection accuracy using free-response receiver operating characteristic (FROC) analysis. MAIN RESULTS: BTU-Net was the only model performing on par with human readers, showing robust sensitivity across the entire range of segmentation probabilities. At 1.5 false positives per projection rate (FPPR), BTU-Net outperformed other models with sensitivity of 0.529 ± 0.026, On a separate hold-out set of low likelihood of disease patients (n=430), the lowest FPPR was 0.08 ± 0.01 for BTU-Net (P<0.0001). SIGNIFICANCE: BTU-Net enables rapid, consistent, and accurate interpretation of planar V/Q scans. Such tools may enhance diagnostic efficiency, standardize reporting, and support non-expert readers in evaluating PE.

articles.title: The evolution of radiographers-an investigation into radiographers' role and perspectives: a EuroAIM/EFRS survey.
articles.abstract: Radiographers play a central role within clinical imaging and radiotherapy teams, acting as a key interface between patients and increasingly complex technologies. As healthcare systems evolve, their scope of practice is expanding alongside advances in digital workflows, artificial intelligence (AI) and new models of care. This EuroAIM/EFRS survey provides a comprehensive European overview of radiographers' roles, professional autonomy, research engagement and perspectives on AI. Based on responses from 1548 radiographers across multiple countries, the findings highlight substantial clinical autonomy and strong responsibility for image quality optimisation and radiation protection, alongside limited but growing involvement in research activities. More than half of the participants expressed interest in greater research participation, indicating a gap between current opportunities and professional aspirations. Responses regarding AI were generally positive, with many participants expecting it to enhance their professional roles, although expectations regarding its workforce impact remained heterogeneous. The survey also confirms the lasting effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on professional practice and highlights variability in perceived career development opportunities. These findings describe a profession in transition, characterised by increasing responsibilities and technological integration and underscore the need for continued investment in education, structured career frameworks and research capacity to support radiographers in an increasingly complex healthcare environment. KEY POINTS: Question What are radiographers' current roles, autonomy, research engagement and perspectives on emerging technologies within a changing imaging and radiotherapy workforce? Findings In 1548 participants, radiographers reported substantial autonomy and responsibility, limited research involvement, positive but heterogeneous AI expectations and variable career opportunities. Critical Relevance Statement This EuroAIM/EFRS survey informs radiology practice by identifying radiographers' professional development, education and research needs and by supporting structured career frameworks and interprofessional workforce planning.

articles.title: Small poorly differentiated synovial sarcoma with concentric periarterial growth causing popliteal arterial stenosis: a case report.
articles.abstract: Soft-tissue sarcomas arising in the popliteal fossa are uncommon but clinically important because of their close relationship to major neurovascular structures. Poorly differentiated synovial sarcoma is an aggressive histologic subtype of synovial sarcoma. We report a case of a small poorly differentiated synovial sarcoma located in the perivascular region of the popliteal fossa that showed concentric periarterial growth with popliteal arterial stenosis. A 68-year-old woman reported a several-month history of heaviness in the right lower extremity. Ultrasonography revealed a 2-cm irregular hypoechoic solid mass circumferentially surrounding the popliteal artery, with no definite internal Doppler flow. The lesion showed intermediate signal intensity on T1-weighted images and heterogeneous intermediate-to-high signal intensity on fat-suppressed T2-weighted images. MRI showed circumferential arterial encasement with stenosis. Non-contrast-enhanced quiescent-interval slice-selective (QISS) MRA helped define the longitudinal extent of popliteal arterial narrowing. Surgical resection required vascular resection and reconstruction bypass of the popliteal artery and vein. Histopathological examination showed nested proliferation of tumor cells with ovoid-to-round nuclei in a hyalinized fibrous stroma. Immunohistochemistry showed positivity for SS18-SSX and SSX, supporting the diagnosis of synovial sarcoma. This case illustrates that even a small synovial sarcoma in the popliteal fossa can circumferentially encase the popliteal artery and cause stenosis.

articles.title: Long-term MRI surveillance of hepatocellular adenomas selected for conservative management: time to regression after oral contraceptive cessation.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To describe the long-term MRI evolution of hepatocellular adenomas (HCAs) selected for conservative management and to quantify the time to predefined degrees of lesion size reduction after oral contraceptive pill (OCP) cessation. METHODS: In this retrospective study, adults with pathologically proven or imaging-typical HCA who underwent serial liver MRI between January 2010 and December 2024 were reviewed. Up to three indexed lesions per patient were tracked, and lesion evolution was categorized using predefined lesion-level size-change thresholds derived from RECIST 1.1 conventions. In lesions from patients with documented post-diagnosis OCP cessation, time to ≥ 10%, ≥ 20%, and ≥ 30% diameter reduction was estimated using Kaplan-Meier analysis. Primary outcomes were repeated in one-lesion-per-patient sensitivity analyses (largest lesion per patient). RESULTS: 116 patients (110 women; mean age 38 ± 10 years) with 269 HCAs; median follow-up 6.5 years. Among 174 lesions selected for continued conservative management, 166 (95.4%) were stable or regressed. In an exploratory subgroup of 17 lesions with baseline diameter ≥ 5 cm, all were stable or regressive and 11 (64.7%) measured below 5 cm at last imaging. Among 81 lesions after OCP cessation, median times to ≥ 10%, ≥ 20%, and ≥ 30% diameter reduction were 8.6, 24.3, and 49.9 months (95% CI for ≥ 30%, 36.2-75.1). Findings were similar in sensitivity analyses. Both observed malignant transformations occurred in β-catenin-activated HCA, with no surveillance hemorrhage. CONCLUSION: In this selected surveillance cohort, most HCAs managed without intervention remained stable or decreased in size during long-term MRI follow-up. After OCP cessation, regression was gradual, with modest reduction often apparent within the first year but larger reductions frequently requiring several years; findings in the small ≥ 5 cm subgroup were exploratory. Limited early size reduction should therefore not, in isolation, be interpreted as failure of conservative management.

articles.title: Reassessing the diagnostic value of spectral CT-derived parameters for pathological grading of urothelial carcinoma of the bladder.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the diagnostic performance of spectral CT-derived quantitative parameters for preoperative prediction of pathologic grade in urothelial carcinoma of the bladder (UCB) and to assess their incremental value over clinical variables and model robustness. METHODS: In this retrospective study, patients with pathologically confirmed UCB who underwent preoperative contrast-enhanced spectral CT were included. Quantitative spectral parameters were extracted. Inter-reader agreement was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs). Variables with P < 0.10 on univariable analysis were entered into multivariable logistic regression to construct clinical, imaging and combined models. Model robustness was evaluated using penalized regression (LASSO and elastic net) as sensitivity analyses. Model performance and clinical net benefit were assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, DeLong testing, and decision curve analysis (DCA). RESULTS: A total of 120 patients were included (65 high-grade tumours and 55 low-grade tumours). Spectral parameters showed good to excellent inter-reader agreement. Several imaging features were associated with tumor grade on univariable analysis (P < 0.05). After inclusion of calcification in the clinical analysis, age remained independently associated with tumor grade, whereas tumor size, tumor number, and calcification were not statistically significant in the multivariable clinical model. AEF remained the only independent imaging predictor. The AUC was 0.743 for the imaging model, 0.746 for the clinical model and 0.772 for the combined model. The incremental improvement of the combined model over the clinical model was small (ΔAUC = 0.027) and not statistically significant (DeLong P = 0.563). DCA showed limited additional net benefit of the combined model at intermediate risk thresholds. CONCLUSION: Spectral CT-derived parameters are associated with pathologic grade in UCB but demonstrate only moderate discriminatory performance.

articles.title: CT imaging features in prognostic risk stratification compared to clinical staging in resectable gastric cancer: a multicenter study.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To evaluate the incremental prognostic value of visually assessable CT features beyond clinical stage (cStage) for disease-free survival (DFS) risk stratification in gastric cancer. METHODS: Patients undergoing curative gastrectomy were retrospectively included in development and external cohorts. Clinical and pathological stages were reconstructed according to the AJCC 8th edition and simplified to three tiers. Clinical Stage, CT Imaging, and Combined models were evaluated for discrimination, calibration, bootstrap-corrected performance, and external validation. Incremental prognostic value was assessed using changes in the C-index and time-dependent AUCs. A development-derived CT Imaging Score (CIS) cutoff was locked for exploratory risk refinement within preoperative cStage strata. RESULTS: Among 886 patients (development, n = 698; external, n = 188), cStage-pStage concordance was 51.0% and 61.2%, respectively (linear-weighted κ = 0.387 and 0.513). In the development cohort, adding CIS to cStage increased the C-index from 0.648 to 0.805 (ΔC-index = 0.160, P = 0.002) and the 1-, 3-, and 5-year AUCs by 0.159, 0.184, and 0.193, respectively (all P = 0.001). The optimism-corrected C-index was 0.797 for the Combined model. External C-indices were 0.676, 0.694, and 0.695 for the Clinical Stage, CT Imaging, and Combined models, respectively. In the development cohort, CIS-high status was associated with worse DFS within cStage II (HR = 8.66, 95% CI: 5.59-13.42) and cStage III (HR = 5.78, 95% CI: 3.74-8.92), with associations retained after adjustment for postoperative pStage. CONCLUSION: Integrating visually assessable CT imaging features with conventional cStage improved DFS prognostic discrimination in the development cohort, while the derived CIS further refined risk stratification within preoperative cStage groups.

articles.title: Very short flow diverters for intracranial aneurysms: technical feasibility, angiographic outcomes, and clinical safety across diverse cerebrovascular locations.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Longer flow diverters (FDs) are often selected to facilitate deployment. Very short FDs (VSFDs; 10-12 mm) offer a targeted alternative, but technical complexity has limited their adoption, resulting in scarce clinical data. METHODS: This single-center, retrospective cohort study included patients with intracranial aneurysms who underwent VSFD treatment. The primary outcome was technical success, defined as deployment of the intended VSFD across the aneurysm neck with complete neck coverage at the end of the index procedure, and analyzed per index aneurysm. Secondary outcomes included angiographic results, assessed using the O'Kelly-Marotta (OKM) grading scale, and clinical outcomes, evaluated with the modified Rankin Scale (mRS) during follow-up. Statistical analyses were performed using R software (version 4.5.2; R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). RESULTS: Seventy-five patients harboring 151 aneurysms were included, with 86 index aneurysms treated using 93 VSFDs. Technical success was achieved in 82 of 86 index aneurysms (95.3%); the remaining 4 aneurysms required a second device because of malposition of the first. At a mean follow-up of 15.2 ± 11.0 months, complete occlusion was achieved in 42 of 49 patients with imaging follow-up (85.7%) and adequate occlusion in 49 of 49 (100%); imaging follow-up was unavailable in 26 of 75 patients (34.7%), so these proportions apply to the imaged subgroup only. Favorable clinical outcome (mRS 0-2) was obtained in 51 of 61 patients with clinical follow-up (83.6%), and no retreatment was required during follow-up. Postprocedural permanent neurological complications occurred in 5 of 75 patients (6.7%). CONCLUSIONS: VSFDs were technically feasible in selected intracranial aneurysms. Whether they offer any advantage over conventional-length devices was not tested in this study and requires anatomically matched comparison. Device malposition occurred only in the middle cerebral artery territory, and in every case the device had been deployed too proximally, so deployment from distal to proximal by experienced operators is essential.

articles.title: MRI-based severity classification of central canal stenosis using radiomics features and machine learning.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Accurate assessment of lumbar degenerative disease is important for treatment planning and surgical decision-making. In this study, we investigated whether radiomics features extracted from lumbar MRI, combined with machine learning models, could be used to classify the severity of lumbar spinal stenosis. MATERIALS AND METHODS: We analyzed 1,500 sagittal T2/STIR-weighted lumbar MRI images representing three categories of central canal stenosis severity: normal/mild, moderate, and severe. Two experienced radiologists manually segmented the sagittal slices, and radiomics features were extracted from each region of interest. These features were used to train and evaluate four machine learning models: random forest (RF), adaptive boosting (AdaBoost), extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), and an artificial neural network (ANN), for stenosis severity classification. RESULTS: All models demonstrated high classification performance, with AdaBoost achieving the highest overall effectiveness. Specifically, AdaBoost reached an accuracy of 80% (95% CI: 75.47-84.53%) and a precision of 81% (95% CI: 76.56- 85.44%). The multi-class Area Under the Curve (AUC) values were 93.60% (95% CI: 90.83- 96.37%) for AdaBoost, 92.80% (95% CI: 89.88-95.72%) for XGBoost, 92.60% (95% CI: 89.64- 95.56%) for RF, and 90.70% (95% CI: 87.41-93.99%) for ANN. While AdaBoost led in discrimination, the ANN model achieved the highest specificity at 90% (95% CI: 86.60-93.40%). CONCLUSION: The results of this study support the feasibility of using radiomics-based machine learning for severity classification of central canal stenosis on lumbar MRI. Although the findings are encouraging, the current workflow relies on manual segmentation and should be regarded as an exploratory proof of concept. Further work is needed to evaluate generalizability and to integrate automated methods suitable for clinical use.

articles.title: One-hour pulsatility index as an independent predictor of futile recanalization after successful mechanical thrombectomy: A prospective observational study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Futile recanalization (FR) - poor functional outcome despite successful mechanical thrombectomy - affects approximately 40% of patients with anterior circulation large vessel occlusion. Reliable bedside predictors of FR at the time of recanalization remain lacking. METHODS: This single-center prospective observational study enrolled 122 consecutive patients with successful thrombectomy (mTICI ≥2b; all mTICI 2b cases corresponded to eTICI 2b67) between 1 October 2025 and 12 April 2026. Pre-procedural optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD) was measured by ultrasound, and post-procedural transcranial color-coded Doppler measurements were obtained by an investigator who was not involved in the endovascular procedure and was blinded to the thrombectomy technique and angiographic reperfusion findings. FR was defined as 90-day mRS 3-6. Discriminative performance was assessed by ROC analysis with DeLong comparison; independent predictors by multivariable logistic regression with bootstrap validation (5000 resamples). RESULTS: FR occurred in 48 patients (39.3%). The 1-hour symptomatic-hemisphere pulsatility index (PI) was markedly elevated in FR patients (1.23 vs. 0.81; p < 0.001; AUC 0.922, 95% CI 0.861-0.984). At a threshold > 0.99, sensitivity was 91.7% (95% CI: 80.4-96.7%) and specificity 89.2% (95% CI: 80.1-94.4%).Preoperative ONSD was also higher in FR patients (5.2 vs. 4.7 mm; p < 0.001; AUC 0.785). The combined model reached AUC 0.934, without significant incremental gain over PI alone (p = 0.062). On multivariable analysis, 1-hour PI (OR 2.929; p < 0.001) and admission NIHSS (OR 1.457; p = 0.009) were independent predictors. Predictive accuracy was preserved in the local anesthesia subgroup (AUC 0.895). CONCLUSIONS: The 1-hour symptomatic PI was independently associated with futile recanalization and showed high discriminatory performance after thrombectomy. Preoperative ONSD may provide complementary risk stratification. Multicenter external validation is warranted.

articles.title: Analysis on radiation protection of FLASH treatment in conventional proton therapy facilities.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: FLASH radiotherapy is an advanced radiotherapy technique featuring ultra-high dose-rate irradiation. Previous preclinical studies have shown that it can significantly reduce damage to normal tissues while preserving the ability to kill tumor cells. Due to the very high current intensity of FLASH radiotherapy, the effectiveness of radiation shielding in current proton therapy facilities needs to be evaluated prior to clinical studies. PURPOSE: Based on the existing shielding conditions of a ProBeam proton therapy system for conventional proton therapy treatment, we studied the shielding effectiveness of FLASH treatment in both the transmission and Bragg-peak modes. METHODS: Under the conditions of single-point irradiation using a proton beam with the highest clinical energy of 244MeV, and the beam intensity of 5nA, 10nA, and 20nA at the nozzle, the ambient equivalent dose rate outside the shielding door was measured with neutron and γ detector, in order to determine the linear relationship between the current intensity and the ambient dose rate. In addition, a gantry room was used as the study object, and the layout design of the points of interest was carried out according to the layout of the proton treatment facility and the transport path and direction of the proton beam, and the most unfavorable working conditions were set for each point of interest. The beam energy was set to 244 MeV, with a cylindrical water phantom (20 cm in diameter) and a solid water block (40 × 40 × 40 cm3) placed at the isocenter. The current at the nozzle was set to 20 nA, and comprehensive environmental dose rate measurements were carried out for the proton radiation workplace. RESULTS: A linear relationship was observed between nozzle current and ambient dose equivalent rate. Based on the linear relationship, when the current was extrapolated to a FLASH current of 170 nA, the measured instantaneous dose rates at some locations were relatively high, with the maximum value of 74.04 µSv/h recorded outside the shielding door. Under the conservative assumption that the total annual beam delivery time is 5 h (treating 6 patients per hour), the maximum annual occupational exposure doses for radiation workers under the transmission and Bragg Peak modes are 0.370 mSv and 0.236 mSv, respectively, which are well below the annual occupational dose limit. CONCLUSIONS: The results indicate that, under existing conventional shielding conditions, the radiation risk posed to the environment outside the treatment room by FLASH irradiation using the Varian ProBeam proton therapy system is safe and controllable, and the annual occupational radiation dose for radiation workers is well below the annual dose equivalent limit. This provides important radiation safety justification for the clinical implementation of FLASH technology in existing proton therapy facilities.

articles.title: A cell-type resolved proton RBE model for potential clinical application.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Despite decades of effort, researchers have failed to develop a clinically implementable Relative Biological Effectiveness (RBE) model that can improve dose accuracy in proton therapy. A key challenge is that RBE's dependence on cell-type is not well understood. This study aimed to overcome this challenge. METHODS: A total of 139 eligible experimental datasets covering 33 cell lines from the Particle Irradiation Data Ensemble (PIDE) database were used in this study. A Poisson-based cell survival model, which has two new parameters α and β conceptually different from that in the conventional LQ model, was used to derive a proton RBE model by globally fitting the proton experimental data. The two parameters' fitting values for a cell's photon data, αX and βX, were used to characterize the cell type. RBE's dependence on cell type was investigated by studying RBE variation on αX and βX. RESULTS: The Poisson-based model showed better global fitting than the LQ model (RMSEw = 6.4% vs. 7.8%, p = 0.00003). A comprehensive RBE model expressed as RBE (LET, DP, αX, βX) was consequently derived. Interestingly, RBE appears to vary minimally within 95% CI of αX variation, while vary greatly for βX variation. Cells were divided into two groups according to βX, and the comprehensive model was simplified into a cell-type resolved model by establishing two cell-type-independent models for the two groups, respectively. This cell-type resolved model shows better agreement with experimental data than the comprehensive model derived from the LQ model. CONCLUSION: The variation of βX, which represents a cell's repair capability for critical damages, mainly contributes to RBE's cell-type dependence. A cell-type resolved model agreeing well with experimental data has been established.
